extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and systematic naturalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on forming natural classifications (especially series-based classifications for investigating particular phenomena) and a taxonomy of common fallacies in reasoning; aimed at teaching how to construct useful classifications and how to detect systematic errors in inference. Contains principles, examples, and a proposed taxonomy of fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification groups by most important common properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of Classification ... is to make us think of those objects together which have the greatest number of important common properties; and which, therefore, we have oftenest occasion, in the course of our inductions, for taking into joint consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form groups so that ideas of objects are brought into the order most conducive to successful inductive inquiry; prioritize properties that matter for induction rather than incidental similarities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the phenomenon as the groundwork for special-purpose classification
rubrics_metrics.description: When the purpose is to facilitate some particular inductive inquiry, ... the very phenomenon or set of phenomena in question must be chosen as the groundwork of the classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For classifications intended to illuminate a specific law, base the grouping explicitly on the phenomenon whose laws are being investigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include all kinds exhibiting the phenomenon regardless of other properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The requisites of a classification intended to facilitate the study of a particular phenomenon, are, first to bring into one class all Kinds of things which exhibit that phenomenon, in whatever variety of forms or degrees;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not exclude instances that show the phenomenon in atypical combinations or low degrees; inclusion supports identification of variation and boundary cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange kinds in a series by degree of the phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondly, to arrange those Kinds in a series according to the degree in which they exhibit it, beginning with those which exhibit most of it, and terminating with those which exhibit least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order instances from highest to lowest degree of the phenomenon to make concomitant variations visible and to facilitate inductive inferences about laws and causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange to enable the Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: This is merely saying that we should put the instances, from which the law is to be inductively collected, into the order which is implied in one of the four Methods of Experimental Inquiry ... the fourth Method, that of Concomitant Variations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use series-ordering that reveals facts which increase or diminish together; such co-variation strongly indicates causal connection or common cause and is often the only practicable method when artificial experiments are limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume a type-species to recognize identity across degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a classification of this sort ... requires the power of recognizing the essential similarity of a phenomenon, in its minuter degrees and obscurer forms, with what is called the same phenomenon in the greatest perfection of its development; ... the assumption of a type-species is indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select as type the kind exhibiting the constitutive properties in the highest degree; treat other varieties as degenerations from that type to help detect rudimentary instances and allied effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary divisions grounded on variations in the main phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary divisions must be grounded not on all distinctions indiscriminately, but on those which correspond to variations in the degree of the main phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When breaking a series into Classes/Orders, cut where conspicuous changes in miscellaneous properties accompany a change in the main phenomenon's intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivide families to reflect contiguous positions on the scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Each family should, if possible, be so subdivided, that one portion of it shall stand higher and the other lower, though of course contiguous, in the general scale;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer subdivisions that preserve the series order (higher vs lower contiguous parts). Only use characters unconnected with the main phenomenon when no connection-preserving split is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize main phenomenon over incidental characters
rubrics_metrics.description: When the principal phenomenon so far transcends in importance all other properties ... any considerable deviation from the rule ... is in general sufficiently guarded against by the first principle of a natural arrangement, that of forming the groups according to the most important characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting incidental properties (e.g., mode of alimentation) unduly determine groupings when they do not track the main phenomenon relevant to the inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply natural-arrangement principles across domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the scientific arrangements of organic nature afford as yet the only complete example ... those principles are applicable to all cases in which mankind are called upon to bring the various parts of any extensive subject into mental co-ordination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the same criteria (type, main phenomenon, series ordering) when organizing non-biological corpora (e.g., codes of law, art, business classifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy of reasoning must include fallacies
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosophy of reasoning, to be complete, ought to comprise the theory of bad as well as of good reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When teaching or assessing reasoning, present both correct methods and systematic errors to give practitioners a practical safeguard against being seduced by apparent evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on systematic (fundamental) bad reasoning, not mere lapses
rubrics_metrics.description: In the present treatise our attention is required, not to mere inexpertness in performing the operation in the right way ... but to the modes of performing it in a way fundamentally wrong;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish accidental mistakes (attention, haste) from fallacies rooted in wrong methods; the latter call for philosophical analysis and classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish moral vs intellectual sources of error
rubrics_metrics.description: The sources of erroneous opinions are twofold, moral and intellectual. Of these, the moral do not fall within the compass of this work. They may be classed under two general heads: Indifference to the attainment of truth, and Bias;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing error, treat moral causes (bias, indifference) as predisposing factors that operate through intellectual failures (e.g., accepting insufficient evidence), rather than as direct logical causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalog apparent evidence that is not real evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A catalogue of the varieties of apparent evidence which are not real evidence, is an enumeration of Fallacies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify fallacies either by the cause that makes something appear evidentiary or by the particular kind of evidence it simulates; this provides a workable taxonomy of fallacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fallacies of Inference from Fallacies of Simple Inspection (a priori)
rubrics_metrics.description: This gives rise to the first great distinction, that between Fallacies of Inference and Fallacies of Simple Inspection. ... This class ... comprehending the whole of what may be termed Natural Prejudices, and which I shall call indiscriminately Fallacies of Simple Inspection or Fallacies a priori, shall be placed at the head of our list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the erroneous belief arises from a mistaken inference from evidence, or from acceptance on mere inspection/presumption without extrinsic evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize Fallacies of Confusion (vagueness and shifting premises)
rubrics_metrics.description: This gives existence to a class of fallacies which may be justly termed ... Fallacies of Confusion; comprehending ... all those which have their source in language, whether arising from the vagueness or ambiguity of our terms, or from casual associations with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether premises are conceived steadily and with due fixity; watch for unconscious substitution of premises or conclusions, and for ambiguities in terms that disguise the error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate fallacies by whether apparent evidence is particulars or general propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Apparent Evidence may be either particular facts, or foregone generalizations; that is, the process may simulate either simple Induction or Deduction;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this axis to subdivide fallacies into Fallacies of Induction vs Fallacies of Deduction, and then further by whether the evidence is false or true-but-inconclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Observation: check accuracy and sufficiency of observed facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies of Induction, where the facts on which the induction proceeds are erroneous, may be termed Fallacies of Observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider malobservation, non-observation, and inference-from-marks as causes; ensure facts are correctly ascertained before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Generalization: avoid unwarranted general conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: The other class of inductive fallacies, in which the facts are correct, but the conclusion not warranted by them, are properly denominated Fallacies of Generalization;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the correct facts actually support the proposed general rule—watch for over-broad extrapolation from limited instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Ratiocination: premises may be true but fail to support conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: There remain ... those in which the premises of the ratiocination do not bear out its conclusion; the various cases, in short, of vicious argumentation, provided against by the rules of the syllogism. We shall call these, Fallacies of Ratiocination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the logical validity/syllogistic form: even true premises must be examined for whether they entail the asserted conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for suppressed (tacit) premises when testing arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: In all arguments, everywhere but in the schools, some of the links are suppressed; ... it is in those steps of the reasoning which are made in this tacit and half-conscious, or even wholly unconscious manner, that the error oftenest lurks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To detect sophistry, supply the unstated premises that the arguer relies upon; check whether those premises are true and whether they actually support the conclusion.
